To the best of our knowledge, this is the first epidemiological, nationally representative, population-based survey on autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) in Vietnam. The survey was conducted by implementing a two-step ASD diagnostic procedure: Phase I using M-CHAT to identify high-risk children in the general population, and Phase II using comprehensive diagnostic assessment criteria (DSM-IV) to confirm the ASD diagnosis. The overall ASD prevalence in children aged 18 and 30 months is 0.758%, that is, 1 in 132 children. Our finding is similar to the estimate of ASD prevalence in other low- and middle-income countries such as China, but slightly lower than that rate in high-income countries such as Canada (1.59%), US (1.68%), Japan (1.8%). Furthermore, our results indicate a much higher prevalence reported by previous small-scale in Vietnam such as 0.46% in National Hospital of Pediatrics in 2007 or 0.50% in 2014. This suggests that ASD should be recognized as a fast-growing issue of national public health concern in Vietnam. Therefore, ASDs are one of the greatest burdens of disease amongst children in Vietnam. The government and relevant stakeholders in Vietnam should prioritize actions to address the developmental and mental health needs of affected children and their families.

In Vietnam, routine screening for ASDs in both low- and highrisk children does not exist. As M-CHAT screening is collected from parents and/or caregivers of the children, self-administered survey could provide inaccurate information if their children are thought to be low risk for ASDs. Furthermore, the completion rate is low even in high-risk populations. As such, it is challenging to collect accurate data from parent self-administered instruments and the data may be less reliable. In line with other countries, Vietnamese parents prefer face-to-face interviews to self-administered interviews. This has been documented in the previous surveys of M-CHAT in Turkey and Thailand. To address this concern, in our study, trained health staff were recruited to conduct face-to-face interviews with the parents to improve the diagnostic predictive power, which is recommended in both high- and lowrisk children. For future studies in Vietnam, we recommend to apply the screening process by semi-structured interviews to improve overall sensitivity and specificity of the M-CHAT. This suggestion is also highlighted in other studies in Thailand or South Korea.

section: Key words > Design and methods > Measurements of ASD > Phase 1: Screening
content: After a thorough review of different ASD screening tools, the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT) was utilized for the screening phase of our study. This tool was also the most common and easy-to-use for early ASD screening in children aged 16 and 30 months in both primary and tertiary health facilities. However, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has issued guidelines for ASD screening at 18 and 24 months since there had evidence for efficacy of screening in community settings. M-CHAT is a self-administered parental questionnaire consisting of 23 (yes-no) items. The M-CHAT is available in at least 22 languages including Vietnamese. Validation studies show the positive predictive value (PPV) of M-CHAT varies from 0.57 to 0.65 in low-risk samples. From a public health perspective, using M-CHAT improves early ASD detection for the entire population while being an easy-to-perform and low-cost tool. In Vietnam, M-CHAT is the main screening tool for children 16-30 months used in both primary and tertiary hospitals with a higher PPV (0.7583) than the PPV in other high-income countries. In our study, M-CHAT-R/F was not chosen as these tools require much more time and resource for follow-up screening. All screenings were conducted by a trained health staff with the participation of the children’s parents and/or caregivers.

content:
As newer, often observation-based or digitally integrated tools emerge, the comparative advantage of the M-CHAT-R/F’s predictive value is increasingly challenged.

Recent advancements suggest that parental assessment can be significantly improved through digital technology. A digital version of the M-CHAT-R/F equipped with automated risk assessment has been shown to improve the overall quality of screening. For instance, the SenseToKnow mobile autism screening application displays strategically designed movies and a bubble-popping game on a caregiver’s screen while recording the child’s behavioural responses through the device’s front-facing camera and sensors. These responses are then subsequently analysed automatically using computer vision and machine learning.

A key factor influencing the tool’s effectiveness is that the M-CHAT-R/F’s screening accuracy is reduced as the child’s age increases, particularly beyond the validated window of 16 to 30 months. Sensitivity reduces and specificity increases for the M-CHAT-R/F as the children grow older. Younger children with general developmental delays may fail certain M-CHAT items even though they are not autistic, as they tend to acquire developmental skills gradually over time. The M-CHAT-R/F’s capacity to detect true positives decreases as the tool becomes less appropriate with developmental milestones relevant for older children. As children grow older, some autism-related behaviours may become less obvious or be masked by learnt behaviours, reducing the likelihood that parents will accurately report the symptoms. Children with milder forms of ASD may acquire compensatory abilities as they grow older, resulting in negative outcomes on an autism screening test. This phenomenon underscores the importance of early and repeated screening to capture evolving symptom presentations, as well as the potential for diagnostic drift in older children for further intervention. The review’s results indicate that this profile, marked by inconsistent sensitivity and low PPV, suggests that while the M-CHAT-R/F can be effective for broad early detection, it may come at the cost of a potentially high burden of false positives.

Furthermore, methodological differences across studies, particularly the use of cross-sectional designs, likely contribute to an overestimation of the M-CHAT-R/F’s sensitivity and specificity values in some published findings. Higher sensitivity in cross-sectional studies is often due to incomplete follow-up on screen negatives and differences in case ascertainment methodology, which prospective studies systematically address. Thus, sensitivity can appear overestimated in cross-sectional studies for M-CHAT R/F. A cross-sectional study conducted among a high-likelihood population increases the chances that positives were truly positive, hence yielding a high sensitivity result. The cross-sectional design resulted in incomplete follow-up of screen-negative cases, as only screen-positive children were referred for diagnostic confirmation. This may have led to an overestimation of sensitivity and the omission of potential false-negative cases.

A score of 8 or higher indicates high risk, and the follow-up interview can be bypassed in favor of immediate referral for early intervention services and diagnostic evaluation. The M-CHAT-R/F takes about 10 min to complete.

The validation sample for the M-CHAT-R/F was large (Robins et al., 2014), and the internal consistency reliability of M-CHAT-R/F is acceptable (Cronbach’s α = 0.79; Robins et al., 2014) as are sensitivity (0.85) and specificity (0.99) values (Robins et al., 2014). The positive-predictive value (PPV) is 0.48 for autism and 0.95 for any developmental disorder (Robins et al., 2014), indicating that 48% of the children who screened positive received an ASD diagnosis and 95% of the children had some sort of developmental delay or concerns, including ASD, that warranted referrals to early intervention services (Robins et al., 2014). Similar rates have been found in other countries (PPV for ASD = 0.55, PPV for any developmental disorder = 0.91; Guo et al., 2019). This indicates that the predictive value of the M-CHAT-R/F for any developmental concerns is higher than for autism specifically. Nevertheless, it should be noted that PPVs are impacted by the base rate of the disorder in the sample studied, such that when the prevalence of a disorder is higher, the probability of having the disorder after a positive test is higher (Monaghan et al., 2021). Robins et al. (2014) do not recommend using M-CHAT-R/F as a broader screening tool because its sensitivity for non-ASD delays has not been well studied (e.g., sensitivity for global developmental delays, communication delays, etc.). The M-CHAT-R/F has been translated into more than 40 languages (www.mchatscreen.com) and has demonstrated satisfactory sensitivity and specificity in adaptations in some countries and regions (e.g., Spain, China, Taiwan; Dai et al., 2021). Screening accuracy was shown to be similar across race and ethnic groups in a recent large study (Guthrie et al., 2019).

content: The selection of studies was made using predetermined eligibility criteria. Filters were applied to limit results to English-language peer-reviewed articles published between 1 January 2020 and 9 October 2025. Eligible studies must also have used an observational study approach (cohort, cross-sectional or case–control) and directly compared the screening accuracy of the M-CHAT-R/F to that of other screening tools. Exclusion criteria were letters, case studies, case reports, editorials, or reviews. Additionally, research that emphasised the M-CHAT-R/F method alone without any comparison to other methods or focused on screening for ASD was not included.

The urgency of early detection is underscored by the broader context of youth mental health; recent data highlights the escalating burden of neurodevelopmental and mental health disorders among children globally, and particularly in Asia, making effective primary care screening an imperative public health priority.

Recognising that comprehensive early intervention, especially before 24 months of age—such as Naturalistic Developmental Behavioural Interventions, targeted speech therapy and structured play-based therapies—can significantly enhance cognitive and adaptive skills. Hence, public health initiatives must prioritise timely and effective screening. To address this need, the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-Up (M-CHAT-R/F) has become a prominent two-stage, parent-dependent screening tool. It consists of 20 yes/no questions that take approximately 5 to 10 min for a caregiver to complete, designed for toddlers aged 16 to 30 months. The revision aimed at lowering false-positive results while ensuring high sensitivity. Recent systematic reviews validate its strong psychometric attributes, showing a sensitivity rate of 78% (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91) and a specificity rate of 0.98 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.00), making it highly recommended for early ASD detection.

The M-CHAT-R/F is a key screening tool, distinct from the comprehensive diagnostic instruments required for a formal evaluation. This diagnostic landscape includes gold-standard tools like the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (sensitivity 87%, specificity 75%), the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (sensitivity 89%, specificity 79%) and the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised diagnostic interview. While all are part of the assessment pathway, the M-CHAT-R/F stands out for its suitability for widespread primary care use because it is a concise, parent-completed tool.

Despite the M-CHAT-R/F’s broad acceptance, including its adaptation for diverse cultural contexts like Malaysia, there are still significant gaps in the compiled evidence. Current research shows a considerable variation in outcomes, attributable to differences in study designs, characteristics of the samples and methods of confirming diagnoses. This inconsistency poses challenges for healthcare professionals and policymakers in establishing screening programmes that are based on solid evidence.

The core findings demonstrate that the M-CHAT-R/F functions as a highly sensitive, yet low specificity, screening tool for ASD, a profile that necessitates careful consideration in clinical implementation. While all included studies were rated as high quality based on the JBI checklist, it is important to acknowledge the substantial variation in sample sizes, ranging from 81 to over 11 000 participants. As such, greater weight was placed on findings from large-scale prospective cohorts which provided highly robust, population-level evidence regarding the M-CHAT-R/F’s lower positive predictive value compared with smaller cross-sectional snapshots, reinforcing a cautious interpretation of the tool’s performance.

The American Academy of Paediatrics recommends that effective developmental screening instruments exhibit sensitivity and specificity of at least 70%–80%. The evidence synthesised in this review reveals that the M-CHAT-R/F’s performance did not consistently meet these standards. Although the tool’s validation across multiple languages underscores its cultural adaptability and broad global applicability, the primary weakness identified was its persistently lower specificity and PPV compared with alternative instruments. The review’s results indicate that this profile, marked by inconsistent sensitivity and low PPV, suggests that while the M-CHAT-R/F can be effective for broad early detection, it comes at the cost of an unacceptable burden of false positives, thereby underscoring the need for mandatory multi-stage validation protocols. Similar findings from a meta-analysis of the M-CHAT-R/F revealed a pooled sensitivity of 82.5% and a positive predictive value of 51.2% in low-risk populations, indicating that roughly half of the children with a positive screen will ultimately receive an ASD diagnosis.

However, the M-CHAT-R/F’s reliance on subjective parental or caregiver reports introduces inherent assessor-dependent limitations. Parents may inadvertently underreport symptoms due to a lack of awareness regarding developmental milestones, or they may exhibit leniency in symptom acknowledgement due to cultural stigmas surrounding developmental delays, thereby increasing the risk of false negatives.

Conversely, false positives can also be driven by parental reporting styles. Parents experiencing high anxiety or over-awareness of certain isolated behaviours may tend to over-report a child’s symptoms. Furthermore, first-time parents or those whose children exhibit highly inconsistent skills often report difficulty in accurately completing the M-CHAT-R/F questionnaire, contributing to decreased specificity.

While earlier seminal reviews have firmly established the M-CHAT-R/F as a massive improvement over baseline clinical judgement, the synthesis of recent literature suggests an evolving landscape. As newer, often observation-based or digitally integrated tools emerge, the comparative advantage of the M-CHAT-R/F’s predictive value is increasingly challenged.
